question: Two weeks after undergoing an emergency cardiac catheterization for unstable angina pectoris, a 65-year-old man has decreased urinary output. He takes naproxen for osteoarthritis and was started on aspirin, clopidogrel, and metoprolol after the coronary intervention. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.5°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 128/88 mm Hg. Examination shows mottled, reticulated purplish discoloration of the feet and ischemic changes on the right big toe. His leukocyte count is 16,500/mm3 with 56% segmented neutrophils, 12% eosinophils, 30% lymphocytes, and 2% monocytes. His serum creatinine concentration is 4.5 mg/dL. A photomicrograph of a kidney biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Emergency cardiac catheterization for unstable angina pectoris" -> "possible cholesterol embolization" -> "renal artery occlusion" -> "decreased renal blood flow" -> "acute kidney injury" -> "decreased urinary output" -> "increased serum creatinine" -> "Cholesterol embolization" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Naproxen use for osteoarthritis" -> "possible allergic interstitial nephritis" -> "eosinophils in leukocyte count" -> "renal inflammation" -> "decreased renal function" -> "increased serum creatinine" -> "Allergic interstitial nephritis" -> 70%

CHAIN: "Contrast-induced nephropathy" -> "history of cardiac catheterization" -> "contrast dye exposure" -> "renal vasoconstriction" -> "decreased renal perfusion" -> "acute kidney injury" -> "increased serum creatinine" -> "Contrast-induced nephropathy" -> 90%
analysis: The patient's presentation with decreased urinary output, mottled discoloration of the feet, ischemic changes on the toe, elevated leukocyte count with eosinophils, and elevated serum creatinine after cardiac catheterization is highly suggestive of cholesterol embolization syndrome affecting the kidneys.
